The person I'd like to talk about is a cousin of mine, Duc, who works as a sound designer for video games. He's in his early thirties and lives in Singapore, though he grew up in the same town as me.

His job, essentially, is to create every sound you hear in a game apart from the music. That means footsteps, doors creaking, the wind, weapons, a character breathing when they're tired, all of it. Sometimes he uses recordings from a library, but a surprising amount of it he records himself. He once told me that the sound of a monster's bones breaking in one game was actually him snapping celery in a cupboard at home.

How he got the job is quite an interesting story in itself. He originally studied computer science, and for a while he worked as a fairly ordinary software developer. But he'd always been obsessed with music and recording, so in his spare time he started adding his own sound effects to small games made by friends. He posted some of this work online, and eventually a studio got in touch to ask if he'd do some freelance work. That turned into a full-time job, and he's been there ever since.

As for why I find it interesting, part of it is just the creativity involved. It's a job where you're constantly experimenting and listening to the world in an unusual way. But what really fascinates me is that it's almost invisible work. If he does it well, players never notice it at all; they just feel that the game is convincing. I find it quite inspiring that someone can put so much care into something whose success is measured by people not noticing it. And of course, the celery story doesn't hurt either.
why9: Định nghĩa công việc bằng liệt kê
'That means footsteps, doors creaking, the wind, weapons, a character breathing when they're tired, all of it.' FC: giải thích nghề lạ bằng ví dụ cụ thể, kết bằng 'all of it' rất tự nhiên.
Đảo tân ngữ lên đầu
'a surprising amount of it he records himself' đưa tân ngữ lên trước để nhấn mạnh. GRA: cấu trúc nâng cao, dùng tự nhiên trong văn nói.
Chi tiết hài hước đáng nhớ
Câu chuyện về cần tây ('snapping celery in a cupboard') và nhắc lại ở cuối ('the celery story doesn't hurt either'). FC: tạo sự liên kết đầu cuối, rất tự nhiên.
Trình tự nghề nghiệp mạch lạc

'He originally studied... for a while he worked... so in his spare time he started... eventually a studio got in touch... That turned into a full-time job.' GRA/FC: thì và liên từ thể hiện quá trình rõ ràng.
Nhấn ý nghịch lý
'something whose SUCCESS is measured by people NOT noticing it.' P: nhấn 'success' và 'not', ngắt nhẹ trước 'is measured'. Người học nên tập nhấn từ phủ định khi nó mang ý chính.
p3samples9: Is it more important to have a well-paid job or an interesting one?

I think it depends a lot on where you are in life. If you're struggling to pay rent or supporting a family, a decent salary has to come first; it's hard to enjoy interesting work if you're constantly worried about money. But beyond a certain point, extra income seems to add less and less to people's happiness, whereas spending most of your waking hours on something that bores you takes a real toll. So ideally, I'd say people should aim for a job that pays enough to live comfortably and then prioritise interest. The trouble is, of course, that not everyone has that choice.
Should young people follow their passion when choosing a job?

I'm a bit sceptical of that advice, to be honest. It assumes young people already know what their passion is, and many don't, at least not at eighteen. It also ignores the fact that some passions are very hard to make a living from. In my experience, passion often develops from doing something well, rather than the other way round. So I'd suggest young people choose something they find reasonably interesting and have some aptitude for, then stay open to where it leads. Following curiosity and building skills tends to be more reliable than chasing a single passion from the start.

p2.sample9:
I'd like to talk about the first time I tried durian, the fruit that's famous, or rather infamous, for its smell. It's quite common in Vietnam, but for some reason I'd managed to avoid it until I was about twenty.

It happened in the Mekong Delta, during a trip with a group of university friends. We'd stopped at a fruit orchard owned by the family of one of our classmates, and her father was very proud of his durian trees. So after lunch he brought out a huge one, cut it open right in front of us, and there was really no polite way of refusing.

The first thing, of course, was the smell. People describe it in all sorts of colourful ways, and I won't repeat most of them, but it's a strong, heavy smell, a bit like onions mixed with something very sweet. I remember hesitating for quite a long time, while my friends, who'd all grown up eating it, were laughing at my expression. Eventually I took a small piece. The texture was the real surprise: it was soft and creamy, almost like custard, and the flavour was nothing like the smell. It was rich and sweet, with a slightly nutty, almost savoury undertone.

As for how I felt about it, I'd say it was a genuine shock, but a pleasant one. I wouldn't claim I fell in love with it immediately, but by the third piece I could see why people are so passionate about it. More than the fruit itself, though, it taught me something about first impressions. I'd spent years avoiding it based on a reputation, and it turned out I'd been missing out. These days I'm much more willing to try things I'm unsure about, and durian has become one of my favourite fruits, much to my friends' amusement.
why9: Tự sửa lời để chính xác
'famous, or rather infamous, for its smell' dùng 'or rather' để điều chỉnh từ. LR: phân biệt 'famous' và 'infamous' chính xác, cách tự sửa rất tự nhiên.
Mô tả mùi vị tinh tế
'soft and creamy, almost like custard', 'rich and sweet, with a slightly nutty, almost savoury undertone'. LR: từ vựng mô tả cảm quan chính xác, có mức độ ('slightly', 'almost').
Né tránh khéo léo
'People describe it in all sorts of colourful ways, and I won't repeat most of them' là cách nói hài hước, lịch sự. LR/FC: 'colourful' theo nghĩa bóng (thô tục) dùng đúng.
Từ trải nghiệm đến bài học
'More than the fruit itself, though, it taught me something about first impressions.' FC: phát triển từ chuyện ăn uống sang bài học về định kiến, câu trả lời có chiều sâu.
Nhấn tương phản mùi và vị
'the FLAVOUR was nothing like the SMELL.' P: nhấn hai danh từ đối lập, ngắt nhẹ sau 'flavour'. Người học nên tránh nhấn vào 'nothing like' mà nhấn vào hai đối tượng được so sánh.
p3samples9: Why are some people unwilling to try new foods?

Part of it is probably biological. Humans have evolved to be wary of unfamiliar foods, because historically, eating the wrong thing could make you seriously ill. But a lot of it is cultural and psychological too. If you've grown up with a fairly narrow diet, unfamiliar textures or smells can feel genuinely off-putting, and some people are anxious about looking foolish if they don't like something in front of others. Habit plays a role as well; when you're tired or busy, it's easier to stick with what you know. That said, most people become more adventurous with exposure, especially when they're with people they trust.
Do you think food is an important part of a country's identity?

Absolutely, and I'd say it's one of the most accessible parts. Food carries a lot of history: the ingredients reflect the climate and geography, and many dishes show traces of trade, migration and even colonisation. For people living abroad, it's often the thing they miss most, and cooking traditional food becomes a way of staying connected to home. That said, national cuisines are rarely as fixed or pure as people like to think. Many so-called traditional dishes were adapted from other cultures surprisingly recently. So food is central to identity, but it's an identity that's always been evolving.

p2.sample9:
The photo I'm most proud of is one I took of my grandfather about four years ago, sitting at the small wooden table in his kitchen, reading a newspaper by the window.

It was taken on an ordinary weekday morning when I was visiting my grandparents in the countryside. I was up early, and I wandered into the kitchen while he was having his morning tea. The light was coming in at a very low angle through the window, which had those old wooden shutters, so there were strips of light and shadow across the table and across his face. He had his glasses pushed down his nose and he was completely absorbed in the paper.

As for how I took it, there was nothing sophisticated about it, really. I just had my phone with me. What I did do was resist the temptation to ask him to pose. I stood in the doorway and took about five or six shots very quietly, and he didn't notice at all. Later on, I converted it to black and white, which I think brought out the contrast in the light, but I didn't edit it much beyond that.

The reason I'm proud of it isn't really technical. There's nothing particularly clever about the composition, and the focus is slightly soft. But it captures him exactly as he was, in a way that more formal photos never did. When people pose, they put on a slightly different face. In this one he's just himself, completely unaware of the camera. He passed away last year, and that photo has become very precious to my family. It's now framed in my grandmother's living room, and when people see it, they always say the same thing: that's exactly how he was.
why9: Mô tả ánh sáng chi tiết
'The light was coming in at a very low angle... so there were strips of light and shadow across the table and across his face.' LR/FC: mô tả cụ thể, giúp người nghe 'nhìn' thấy bức ảnh.
Nhấn mạnh bằng trợ động từ 'did'
'What I did do was resist the temptation to ask him to pose.' dùng 'did' nhấn mạnh trong câu chẻ. GRA: cấu trúc nhấn mạnh tự nhiên, đối lập với câu trước 'nothing sophisticated'.
Collocation nhiếp ảnh vừa đủ
'brought out the contrast', 'the composition', 'the focus is slightly soft'. LR: từ chuyên môn dùng đúng và không quá kỹ thuật.
Lý do tự hào không nằm ở kỹ thuật
'The reason I'm proud of it isn't really technical.' rồi giải thích ý nghĩa cảm xúc. FC: trả lời phần 'explain' bằng một góc nhìn bất ngờ, có chiều sâu.
Nhịp chậm khi kể phần cảm xúc

'He passed away last year, / and that photo has become very PRECIOUS to my family.' P: chậm lại, ngắt sau 'last year', nhấn 'precious'. Người học nên bắt chước cách dùng nhịp chậm cho câu mang cảm xúc.
p3samples9: Do you think photos on social media give a true picture of people's lives?

Not really, and I think most people know that, even if they don't always remember it while scrolling. What people post is heavily selected: the holiday, the nice meal, the good hair day, rarely the dull or difficult moments. And with filters and editing, even those moments are often polished. That doesn't make the photos lies exactly; they're real moments, just very unrepresentative ones. The risk is that people compare their ordinary, unedited lives with everyone else's highlights, which can leave them feeling inadequate. There's been a bit of a backlash recently, with people posting more casual, unfiltered content, but the basic tendency hasn't changed.
Should people be allowed to take photos of strangers in public places?

Legally, in most places, they are, and I think that's broadly right. Banning it would make street photography and even simple holiday snaps almost impossible, and some of the most valuable historical photos are of ordinary people in public. But I think there's an important difference between taking a photo and what you do with it. Posting a picture of a stranger online in order to mock them, or using it commercially without permission, is a different matter entirely. So rather than restricting the act of photography, I'd focus on respecting people's dignity, and giving them a clear way to ask for images to be removed.

p2.sample9:
I'd like to talk about the day I found out I'd been accepted onto a master's programme abroad, with a full scholarship. It was about five years ago, and I still remember it in a lot of detail.

I'd applied about six months earlier, and the process had been long and fairly stressful: essays, references, an interview over a very unreliable video call. The results were supposed to come out at the end of March, but the date came and went with nothing. I'd more or less convinced myself that silence meant rejection.

Then, one morning in early April, I was on the bus to work, half asleep, scrolling through my emails, and there it was. The subject line just said 'Your application', which told me nothing. I remember holding my phone for a few seconds before opening it, partly out of nerves and partly because I wanted to delay finding out. When I finally read the first line, which started with 'We are delighted to inform you', I had to read it three times to make sure I hadn't misunderstood.

The first person I told was my mother. I rang her straight away, still on the bus, and probably far too loudly for a crowded bus at eight in the morning. She didn't say anything for a moment, and then she started crying, which set me off as well. After that, I messaged a couple of close friends and my former teacher who'd written one of my references.

As for how I felt, it was a mixture of elation and pure relief. But more than anything, I think it was a sense that all the effort had actually counted for something. And honestly, a part of me was quite scared too, because I suddenly realised it was real, and I'd have to move to the other side of the world.
why9: Tạo kỳ vọng và hồi hộp
'the date came and went with nothing. I'd more or less convinced myself that silence meant rejection.' FC: xây dựng căng thẳng trước khi đến tin tốt, câu chuyện có cao trào.
Cấu trúc 'there it was'
'scrolling through my emails, and there it was.' là cấu trúc đảo ngắn gọn, tạo khoảnh khắc. GRA: dùng đảo ngữ tự nhiên trong văn kể.
Lý do hành động có hai vế
'partly out of nerves and partly because I wanted to delay finding out' dùng cặp 'partly... partly'. GRA/LR: giải thích động cơ tinh tế, hai vế song song.
Từ vựng cảm xúc đa dạng
'elation and pure relief', 'which set me off as well', 'counted for something'. LR: phrasal verb 'set me off' (làm tôi khóc theo) và collocation chính xác.
Nhấn khi chuyển ý
'And HONESTLY, / a part of me was quite SCARED too.' P: ngắt sau 'honestly', nhấn 'scared' để thể hiện cảm xúc trái chiều. Người học nên tập ngắt nhịp trước ý bất ngờ.
Kết bài có cảm xúc đa chiều
Kết bằng nỗi sợ bên cạnh niềm vui: 'I'd have to move to the other side of the world.' FC: không chỉ nói 'I was very happy' mà thể hiện cảm xúc phức tạp, thật hơn.
p3samples9: Why do the media focus more on bad news than good news?

Partly it's simply human nature. We're more alert to threats than to good news, probably for evolutionary reasons, so negative stories grab our attention and get more clicks. Since many media outlets depend on attention for advertising revenue, they have a strong incentive to lead with crises, crime and conflict. There's also a more defensible reason: journalism is supposed to hold power to account, which naturally means highlighting problems. Good news is often gradual, like falling poverty rates over decades, and doesn't fit the format of breaking news. So it's a mix of commercial pressure and the nature of news itself.
Should news programmes include more positive stories?

I think so, within reason. If people are only exposed to bad news, they can end up with a distorted, overly bleak view of the world, and that can lead to apathy, a sense that nothing can be done. Including stories about problems being solved, rather than just problems, can actually make audiences more engaged. That said, positive stories shouldn't come at the expense of serious reporting, and there's a danger of them becoming trivial, heartwarming filler. What I'd like to see isn't fluffy good news, but more reporting on solutions: what's working, where and why.
